messages.subject: Re: questions (new user) re: convergence failure & cluster size
messages.subject_clean: questions (new user) re: convergence failure & cluster size
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jay,

I'll reply to the list, so that my reply is in the archives for others wondering
about the same issues.

Firstly, I did you search, rather than browse the list archives?
(Click on "Search the archives" at
http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling.html)
I ask because I tried typing in "convergence" to the search box and found two
messages that address much of your first question (messages 158 and 548) and
typed in "size bias" to find at least one that addresses your second (message
27).

Have a look at those messages, and then the following.

The first thing you should do, after a detailed exploratory examination of your
data, is think about truncation.  Look under "Truncation" in the index of
Introduction to Distance Sampling for more on this.  Also look under "Analysis,
guidelines" in the book or online help for suggestions about how to approach an
analysis.

If, once you've truncated, you get convergence warnings, you should look and see
which model they occur for.  If you're using sequential selection of adjustment
terms (the default) and it occurs for a model with lots of adjustment terms and
that model is subsequently not selected as it has a higher AIC than one with
fewer adjustments, then there's probably nothing to worry about.  I think I
showed an example of this in either message 158 or 548.  In some rare cases, you
can get convergence problems even for models with few adjustments, particularly
for the hazard rate key function and even more so when you're using covariates
(the MCDS analysis engine).  In this case, you may need to experiment with
setting starting values and/or putting bounds on the parameters.  This is
particularly so for the shape parameter of the hazard rate function (usually
labelled A(2) in the results) for which an upper bound can sometimes need to be
set for data with a "spike" at zero distance.  (In this case, if the "spike" is
due to rounding of distances to zero or to movement of animals onto the line
then converting the data into intervals is a more effective and defensible
solution.)

Regarding the size bias warning; we normally expect large clusters of animals to
be easier to detect than small clusters at large distances, so a regression of
cluster size against distance from the line has a positive slope.  For reasons
outlined in the book (look in the index under "size biased sampling"), the
default regression in Distance is actually log(cluster size) against detection
probability, which we expect to have a negative slope.

In some cases, the estimated slope can go the other way - i.e., the regression
of log(cluster size) against detection probability has a positive slope.  One
obvious reason for this is that the slope is an estimate, subject to sampling
error, so it could just be chance.  Another is that the true slope really is
positive: that you really are more likely to record smaller clusters at greater
distances from the line (and so lower probability of detection).  This can occur
if you underestimate cluster size at these larger distances (can't see the whole
cluster).  The regression still works fine though -- the estimated intercept at
zero distance is still an unbiased estimate of average cluster size in the
population.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Standard Error or Standard Deviation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Not too sure whether I am thinking in the correct lines, wished to have some assistance regarding this issue. We intend to compare two density estimates obtained with the help of this software. For the same, we are computing one factor ANOVA manually.

In distance software, we get the value of SE (Standard Error).
Now for doing ANOVA manually, s2 (s square) is required. Is the standard error itself the s or do we have to use the following relationship:
s2 = n.(SE)2         ...(1)

If this is true, I have a little problem in case of calculation of CV, which is
CV = s / Mean        ...(2)

When we use the above relationship and divide Standard Error by Mean obtained in distance output, we get precisely the CV that is mentioned in the next column of the same output. Now the above two are contradicting and affect results of ANOVA test heavily. The question I have is whether we shall consider SE as s for the manual calculation of ANOVA or calculate its value first by using equation (1)?

Koustubh

messages.subject: Re: Standard Error or Standard Deviation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Koustubh, list,

If you are comparing two density estimates, your single-factor ANOVA is the same
as the t-test described in Section 3.6.5 of Introduction to Distance Sampling.  It
describes there how to obtain the standard error of the difference in densities.
When the two estimates are independent, simply add the variances.  Where they
share some component of estimation (such as f(0)) things are a little more complex
as outlined in the section (although it isn't a good idea to estimate a pooled f
(0) unless you have to, because changes in abundance may then be confounded with
changes in detectability).

The same approach can be taken using ANOVA and you will get the same result.  You
want to use the standard errors of the estimates in calculating the error mean
square.

> >If this is true, I have a little problem in case of calculation of CV, which is
> >CV = s / Mean        ...(2)

On page 424 of the book (the Glossary) we define CV as standard error/estimate.
Either definition is "correct", but it's important to be clear about which one is
being used in a particular context.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

Dear list members,

I would be grateful if someone could give me some light in 2 distance =
sampling related issues.

For primate surveys in the Amazonian forests is quite usual to detect =
some species, e.g. Capuchin Monkeys, sometimes visualy and in other =
instances through auditory cues. Should this sightings be stratified for =
different detenction function curves?

Another thing, perhaps a little more complex: some of this Capuchin =
Monkey groups are eventually detected through auditory cues given by an =
associated species of monkey, the Squirrel Monkey, which in turn is also =
being surveyed. Therefore detection of one species influences detection =
of another.  The opposite relation is also true, but not so frequent. =
Should those be also stratified? What would be the best approach?

Thanks,

Leonardo Fleck

messages.body_plain:
> > I would be grateful if someone could give me some light in 2 distance sampling related issues.
> >
> > For primate surveys in the Amazonian forests is quite usual to detect some species, e.g. Capuchin Monkeys, sometimes visualy and in other instances through auditory cues. Should this sightings be stratified for different detenction function curves?
> >
> > Another thing, perhaps a little more complex: some of this Capuchin Monkey groups are eventually detected through auditory cues given by an associated species of monkey, the Squirrel Monkey, which in turn is also being surveyed. Therefore detection of one species influences detection of another.  The opposite relation is also true, but not so frequent. Should those be also stratified? What would be the best approach?

Probably in both cases, it is worth using the MCDS engine of Distance 4,
with cue type as a factor.  Then look at the fitted detection functions
and use the goodness-of-fit statistics to assess whether you have a good
fit for each cue type.  In fact, pooling robustness means that the
standard approach will probably work OK, provided the detection functions
for different cue types are not too extreme.  You could try analyses with
and without cue type as a factor to check this.

Steve

messages.subject: Pooling of individual transect lengths
messages.body_plain:
We are based in a dry deciduous forest of central India and studying ungulates. A total of 9 line transects between 1.8 and 2.6 km have been laid and are traversed repeatedly about 10 times (total length = approximately 500 km) once a year.
While using the distance 4.0, we face a peculiar problem which seems unaddressed so far.

1.
When we consider the transect lines as spatial replicates and the repitition as temporal, we calculate the total length of one transect as :
Length of Transect (for estimation) = (Length of Transect segment) x (Number of times traversed)

e.g. Length (Transect 1) = (1.8 * 10)

Similarly we do for all transects and represent them in the distance data as 9 different samples.

2.
As another technique, we are calculating the total length of the transects by adding the total length with the number of times they have been traversed. Now we use the data in distance as only single sample (transect) and estimate densities.

The point to remember here is that we are not interested in ecological densities but we wish to estimate population density for biomass estimation and other factors. The influential features are that the lines are randomly laid and not stratified. Is it a good idea to pool the whole length into one before estimating density? Is the technique 2 valid?

The reason why I am curious to learn about validity is that in both the cases there is a tremendous difference in the Standard Error and hence in the Coefficient of Variance which we need later to compare different datasets. When we pool the transect lengths and replications, our CV reduces dramatically as compared to other cases. This could possibly be because all transects are in various strata of different individual species's density.

Looking forward,

Koustubh Sharma

messages.subject: Re: Pooling of individual transect lengths
messages.body_plain:
Koustubh,

You should definitely enter these as 9 different samples, and not pool
into a single sample.  The latter provides Distance with no replication
from which to estimate variance, so it simply uses a Poisson variance by
default.  Almost all real data sets show greater variability than Poisson,
so variance is underestimated when you pool your data.  In your case, the
variance is inflated further because 9 lines is really too few, and the
uncertainty in estimating variance from just 9 lines causes the confidence
intervals to be wider.  So unfortunately, the large variance of your
method 1 is probably a fair reflection of uncertainty, while your method 2
will give variance estimates that are much too small.

Steve

messages.subject: Dist. Sampling and SCFs in Moose surveys
messages.subject_clean: Dist. Sampling and SCFs in Moose surveys
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

I am trying to learn more about aerial-based Moose surveys with DISTANCE
Sampling, and Moose detectability by landcover strata.

I noticed that in the Moose literature a SCF (Sightability Correction
Factor) appears to be widely used.

I am aware of the Pronghorn and some Deer applications with DISTANCE
Sampling; but not much for Moose.

Would you know of DISTANCE Sampling applications for Moose, and how
DISTANCE Sampling performs in comparison to the 'SCF' ?

Are there Moose studies that evaluate detectability etc. with
radio-collared individuals and with Mark-Capture-Recapture approaches ?

Moose seem to congregate during specific seasons; how would DISTANCE
perform in such situations (cluster and distribution issues etc.) ?

Thanks in advance for any insights and experiences.

Kind regards

    Falk

Falk Huettmann
Biology and Wildlife Dept., Institute of Arctic Biology
University of Alaska Fairbanks AK 99775-7000 USA
